Engagement pour un Séjour d’Etudes 
 
Je soussigné …………………………………………………………….. déclare avoir pris connaissance des conditions 
de mobilité en SE suivantes :  
 
 Un seul diplôme : diplôme de Centrale Nantes 
 La mobilité est encadrée et nécessite l’établissement d’un Learning Agreement (LA)  
 La durée est une année complète (S9/S10) 
 60 crédits ECTS à valider dans l’établissement partenaire (intégrant un Master Thesis 
équivalent à un TFE). 
 Le Master Thesis de 5 mois minimum doit être conventionné par l’université d’accueil et 
encadré / évalué par un professeur de l’université d’accueil 
 Le tuteur Centrale Nantes doit être tenu informé des modalités 
 L’établissement d’accueil peut autoriser la réalisation du Master Thesis en partenariat avec 
une entreprise : une convention devra être signée entre l’établissement d’accueil, l’entreprise 
et l’étudiant selon les modalités du pays d’accueil et de l’établissement d’accueil.  
 Centrale Nantes s’engage à reconnaitre l’ensemble des 60 crédits ECTS obtenus (cours  + 
Master Thesis indépendamment de leur répartition) 
 Le TFE (ou son équivalent avec le Master Thesis) étant obligatoire pour l’obtention du diplôme 
d’ingénieur de l’Ecole Centrale de Nantes. A défaut de Master Thesis dans la formation, l’Ecole 
ne reconnaitra que 46 ECTS maximum. 
 Si validation de 46ECTS dans l’université partenaire alors convention possible par Centrale 
Nantes 
 Les résultats obtenus en SE sont soumis à l’approbation du jury de 3e année de Centrale Nantes  
 SI le Master Thesis n’est pas inclus dans les 60 ECTS validés par l’université d’accueil, l’étudiant 
devra réaliser un TFE après les deux semestres d’études. Ce TFE sera conventionné par 
Centrale (3 semestres au total et deux inscriptions à Centrale). 
 
 
Fait à …………………………., le ……………..

Task 2 - Topographical Mapping | 1
 Task 2: Topographical Mapping
Knowledge structure across 31 papers on scheduling, energy, digital twins, reinforcement learning and explainable AI
 Primary region
 Papers
 Interpretation
Thermal and furnace scheduling
 9
Largest process-specific concentration. Strong coverage of furnace and heat-treatment scheduling with energy objectives.
Steelmaking and plant-energy coordination
 7
Connects production operations with plant-wide energy flows, uncertainty and demand response.
Rolling planning and process optimization
 5
Smaller but coherent cluster linking rolling schedules, quality and upstream reheating decisions.
Intelligent and human-centered scheduling
 10
Largest primary region, spanning DRL, digital twins, explainability and human oversight.
Executive findings
- Knowledge is strongly concentrated around thermal-process scheduling: 9 of 31 papers directly address furnaces, reheating or heat treatment.
- Energy is the dominant common objective and creates the strongest links between otherwise separate process areas.
- Digital twins and DRL form an emerging bridge between static optimization and live decision-making.
- Explainability, human oversight and process safety remain comparatively isolated from steel-specific furnace and plant-energy studies.
- The central organizational gap is integration: few papers combine physical process constraints, live plant data, adaptive optimization and human-readable explanations in one system.
Method
Each paper was coded on three dimensions: industrial process, decision objective and analytical method. The hierarchy uses one primary region per paper. The network adds a link
when two papers share at least two substantive tags; only each paper's four strongest relationships are retained for readability. This is a thematic cross-reference network, not a
bibliographic citation network.

Task 2 - Topographical Mapping | 4
 Structural interpretation
Concentrated knowledge
The densest region combines furnace scheduling, energy consumption and
metaheuristic or mathematical optimization. D07, D22 and D27 form a particularly
close heat-treatment subgroup because they jointly address scheduling, energy and
multi-criteria performance.
Bridge papers
D31 - Towards live decision-making for service-based production: Integrated process
planning and scheduling with Digital Twins and Deep-Q-Learning
D26 - Research on modelling and optimization of hot rolling scheduling
D12 - Energy-Efficient Integration Optimization of Production Scheduling and Ladle
Dispatching in Steelmaking Plants
D16 - Human-Centric Job-Shop Production Planning and Scheduling System Based
on the Concept of I5.0
D24 - Optimal scheduling of a by-product gas supply system in the iron- and
steel-making process under uncertainties
Isolated or weakly connected knowledge
The least-connected papers introduce important capabilities that are not yet deeply
integrated into the dominant steel scheduling literature. These include process-safety
governance, virtual-market agent coordination and human-centered Industry 5.0
design.
D25 - Process safety 4.0: Artificial intelligence or intelligence augmentation for safer
process operation?
D19 - IoT-based framework for digital twins in steel production: A case study of key
parameter prediction and optimization for CSR
D11 - Dynamic reallocation and rescheduling of steel products using agents with
strategical anticipation and virtual market structures
D05 - An Uncertainty Involved Two-Stage Energy Optimization Framework Based on
Deep Reinforcement Learning for Steel Enterprise
D14 - GA-BP prediction model for energy consumption of steel rolling reheating
furnace
Implication for Task 3
The strongest divergence to examine is between optimization-first approaches and
learning-enabled live control. A second tension is autonomy versus transparency:
DRL and digital twins improve responsiveness, while XAI and human-in-the-loop
studies expose trust, accountability and safety requirements.

Task 3 - Synthesis Divergence | 1
 Task 3: Synthesis Divergence
Contrasting the approaches in the 31-paper corpus to expose the trade-offs facing an AI-enabled steel scheduling organization
 Task 3 conclusion: the organization should combine constraint-based optimization with adaptive AI, coordinate decisions across processes,
 and retain human authority for safety-critical or high-impact changes.
Purpose
Task 2 identified dense technical clusters but also showed that the literature does not converge on one scheduling philosophy. Task 3 examines the disagreements. The analysis
focuses on three tensions that materially affect implementation: how decisions are computed, how wide the optimization boundary should be, and how much authority AI should
receive.

 Evidence selection and comparison method
Twenty representative papers were selected from the Task 2 map. Selection emphasized papers that sit near the opposite ends of each tension or connect two clusters. Each paper
was compared on decision scope, method, uncertainty treatment, real-time capability, constraint handling, human role, evidence base and limitations.

Interpretation rule
Reported improvements are treated as evidence within each study's own setting, not as directly comparable effect sizes. Differences in plants, problem sizes, objectives and baselines
prevent a valid league table. The synthesis therefore compares capabilities and implementation requirements rather than ranking algorithms by one performance number.


Task 3 - Synthesis Divergence | 4
 Tension 1: Optimization-first versus adaptive AI
 Dimension
 Optimization-first
 Adaptive AI
Decision logic
Explicit objective functions and constraints; exact, robust or metaheuristic search.
Policy learned from data or simulation; action selected from current state.
Best-supported benefit
Feasibility, auditability and reproducibility. D01 embeds furnace dynamics; D29 models
uncertainty explicitly.
Fast online decisions and adaptation. D05 reports less than half manual cost and
roughly 100x solver speed; D09 handles market and process uncertainty.
Main limitation
Model maintenance and computational growth. Simplifying assumptions can narrow
applicability; D23 focuses on a single furnace.
Training burden, transfer risk and weak guarantees outside training conditions. D09
explicitly avoids broad generalization claims.
Human role
Experts formulate constraints, objectives and acceptable trade-offs.
Experts define rewards, training scenarios and intervention limits; D20 uses human
feedback to shape reward design.
Organizational fit
Stable, safety-critical and tightly regulated decisions.
High-frequency decisions in dynamic environments with sufficient data and simulation.
Divergence
Optimization-first papers treat a correct model as the foundation of a good decision. Learning-based papers treat adaptation speed as the foundation. The first risks becoming rigid
when the plant changes; the second risks acting confidently outside its validated operating envelope.
 Required resolution: AI may optimize within a deterministic feasibility envelope, but it must not learn or override metallurgical and safety
 constraints.


Task 3 - Synthesis Divergence | 5
 Tension 2: Local equipment optimization versus plant-wide
 integration
 Dimension
 Local optimization
 Integrated optimization
Scope
One furnace, heat-treatment line or prediction problem.
Linked production stages, logistics, energy flows or process planning.
Evidence
D14 predicts furnace energy at 94.7% accuracy. D27 reports about 10% global-goal
and 6% energy improvement in its casting case.
D12 reports 1.21% energy reduction at constant production efficiency. D17 integrates
reheating and rolling; D24 coordinates gas supply in real time.
Strength
Clear ownership, limited data integration and easier validation.
Avoids shifting costs, delays or energy burdens from one department to another.
Weakness
A locally optimal schedule may create downstream waiting, lateness or instability.
More data dependencies, conflicting objectives and greater computational and
governance complexity.
Implementation condition
Reliable equipment model and local operating data.
Shared data definitions, cross-functional objectives and synchronized planning
horizons.
Divergence
The technical literature often improves one component because the problem is measurable and solvable. The integrated papers show that process interfaces - furnace to rolling,
production to ladles, and production to energy supply - determine whether local savings become plant savings.
 Required resolution: retain local models, but evaluate every schedule against shared plant-level energy, delivery, quality and stability
 objectives.


Task 3 - Synthesis Divergence | 6
 Tension 3: Autonomous decisions versus human oversight
 Issue
 Synthesis
Case for autonomy
DRL, MARL and digital twins can process live state information and react faster than manual scheduling (D09, D21, D31).
Case for oversight
XAI studies show that technically strong decisions can fail adoption when workers cannot understand them (D04, D06). Process-safety research argues for intelligence
augmentation rather than replacement (D25).
Operational evidence
D13 combines explainable methods with MARL production control. D16 reports lower downtime and cycle time when operators are explicitly modeled and supported.
Unresolved risk
Explanations can be plausible without proving safety. Human approval can also become a bottleneck or a rubber stamp if responsibility is unclear.
Decision principle
Authority should depend on consequence, novelty and model confidence - not simply on whether AI can produce a schedule.
 Required resolution: routine decisions can be automated inside validated limits; significant schedule changes require planner approval;
 safety or metallurgical exceptions remain human decisions.

Non-negotiable requirements carried into Task 4
- Zero violations of hard metallurgical, equipment and safety constraints.
- A live and quality-controlled representation of plant state.

- Human override, fallback schedules and a complete decision audit trail.

Task 4 - Integrative Synthesis | 1
 Task 4: Integrative Synthesis
A unified organizational blueprint for intelligent, energy-aware and human-supervised steel production scheduling
 Recommended target: a hybrid scheduling platform in which the digital twin supplies live state, deterministic models enforce feasibility,
 optimization and DRL propose decisions, and humans govern high-impact or exceptional actions.
Design objective
The blueprint integrates the strengths identified in Task 3 without pretending that one algorithm can solve the entire problem. It separates physical truth, hard constraints, decision
intelligence, explanation and organizational authority into explicit layers.

Why the layers matter
The design prevents the AI policy from becoming the source of truth. Physical and metallurgical constraints remain independently maintained and testable. The AI can explore and
adapt, but every proposed action is checked before execution. This preserves the speed benefits of D05, D09, D21 and D31 while answering the safety and accountability concerns in
D04, D06, D16 and D25.

Governance rules
- No model deploys without an identified owner, intended-use statement and validated operating envelope.
- Constraint changes require process-engineering approval and independent regression tests.
- Every executed schedule retains its inputs, model version, alternatives, explanation and human actions.
- Overrides are treated as learning evidence, not as operator failure.
- Automation is suspended when data quality, drift, latency or safety thresholds are breached.

Recommended first pilot
Begin with one reheating or heat-treatment scheduling decision because Task 2 shows the strongest evidence concentration there. Run the system in advisory mode, integrate energy
and delivery objectives, and include one downstream interface such as rolling availability. This creates measurable value without attempting plant-wide autonomy at the outset.
 Scale by adding interfaces, not by replacing the validated core: furnace -> rolling -> ladles -> plant-energy coordination.

Minimum acceptance tests
- Replay historical disturbances and verify that all proposed schedules remain feasible.
- Stress-test missing sensors, delayed data, price spikes, equipment outages and unseen order mixes.
- Compare optimization-only, AI-only and hybrid variants to establish incremental value.
- Require planners to complete scenario-based explanation and override exercises.
- Test fallback schedules and manual recovery before enabling automatic execution.

Final organizational blueprint
The organization should establish a cross-functional scheduling product team rather than treat the solution as a stand-alone AI model. The team owns a continuously validated digital
twin, a deterministic constraint layer, a portfolio of optimization and learning methods, and a human-centered decision interface. Authority expands only after evidence from shadow
and advisory operation demonstrates feasibility, value and user readiness.
 The target is supervised autonomy: rapid machine-supported decisions, bounded by physical rules and accountable human governance.
